A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites so people everywhere can load pages quickly. Without one, every visitor request travels all the way to a single origin server, the original computer where a website's files truly live. That works fine for a small audience, but it gets slow when thousands of people in far-off places ask for the same content at once. A CDN solves this by placing copies of that content at an edge location, a computer positioned close to where the requests actually come from, rather than making every request cross the globe. When someone visits a site, the nearby edge location checks whether it already has a fresh copy stored; if it does, that's called a cache hit, and the page appears almost instantly because nothing had to travel far. If it doesn't have a copy yet, it fetches one from the origin server, delivers it, and keeps a copy for next time. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood bakeries that all sell bread from one central recipe: instead of everyone traveling across town to the original bakery, nearby branches keep fresh loaves ready, only calling the main kitchen when something new needs baking. This arrangement is why videos start almost instantly and news sites load quickly even during huge surges of visitors.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's true files | Everything ultimately comes from here first |
| Edge location | A nearby computer holding copies of the content | Shortens the distance data must travel |
| Cache hit | When a nearby copy is found and used | Makes loading nearly instant |
| CDN | The whole network of edge locations working together | Keeps websites fast and reliable worldwide |
